back: A change in which no new substance is formed (for example melting, boiling, dissolving, crushing). It is usually easy to reverse.
A change in which one or more new substances, with different properties, are formed (for example burning, rusting, cooking). It is usually hard to reverse.

front: List four signs that a chemical change may have taken place.
back: A gas is given off (fizzing); a precipitate forms; a colour change; energy (heat or light) is given out or taken in.

front: What is the one question that always decides whether a change is physical or chemical?
back: Has a new substance been formed? If yes, it is chemical; if no, it is physical.

front: Why does a burning candle show both kinds of change?
back: The wax melts (physical: still wax) and the wax vapour burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water (chemical: new substances).

front: Is dissolving salt in water a physical or a chemical change? Why?
back: Physical: no new substance forms, and evaporating the water gets the salt back.

front: Does an energy change prove that a chemical change has happened?
back: No. Melting, boiling and condensing involve energy changes but are physical; some salts cool water when they dissolve.

front: Sort these: melting wax, burning firewood, souring milk, boiling water, rusting iron.
back: Physical: melting wax, boiling water. Chemical: burning firewood, souring milk, rusting iron.

front: Give four chemical changes you might see at home.
back: Firewood or charcoal burning; milk souring to amasi; an egg cooking; an iron gate rusting (also bread dough rising).

front: Can a chemical change ever be reversed?
back: Some can: heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate gives white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, and adding water turns it blue again. Decide by asking whether a new substance forms.
